title: We spent money and a year testing AI trading. Findings? It can't trade.
author: _foursix_
selftext:
I've posted a few things about our experiments. But here's the free scoop: AI can't trade. We started experiments as early as GPT 4 with image recognition and chart reading. It can read charts, understand everything about trading, but it can't do it. Mostly because the market is a casino these days. We are proving that it is useful for long term, buy and hold, portfolio management. But most people don't care about that, unless it can outperform the market. AI just can't do it. It is an LLM—a LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL which means it doesn't know the next move better than anyone else. It is also very incapacitated by usage costs, no eye-balls to watch the market in real-time, etc. This would be interesting to test perhaps, an AI model watching and trading real-time, basically as fast as it is able to process data (smaller models maybe every few seconds), but the more thinking effort, the longer it takes to process a single snap shot. We can't do that because we found the costs prohibitive. To run an LLM like Gemini flash, grok, GPT constantly on second level data and chart reading on the level of a human day-trader would roughly be this:

An AI that reads the market every second costs roughly $1,000–$50,000 a month depending on the model, and it still couldn't act every second. The cheaper design that actually works is code that watches every tick and calls the AI only when something happens. That costs about $1–25 a month, and we already run a version of it.

I based this on our last 14 days of real usage: 4,549 calls, $43.73. One of the decision calls averages about 22,000 tokens.

**Cost of one session (6.5 hours), by design.** Monthly figures assume 21 trading days.

|Model|Every second, full prompt (/mo)|Every second, slim prompt (/mo)|Supervisor every minute (/mo)|Only when something happens (/mo)|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Ling 3.1 Flash|$903|$85|$15|$0.71|
|Claude Haiku 5.5|$1,351|$123|$23|$0.91|
|DeepSeek V4.1 Flash|$1,686|$158|$28|$1.05|
|GPT-5.6 Luna|$2,850|$256|$48|$1.55|
|Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite|$4,791|$418|$80|$2.38|
|Gemini 3.8 Flash|$10,135|$921|$169|$4.66|
|Grok 4.3|$14,128|$1,351|$235|$6.37|
|Grok 4.7|$24,079|$2,260|$401|$10.62|
|Claude Sonnet 5.5|$27,027|$2,457|$450|$11.88|
|Claude Opus 5.5 / Gemini 4 Argon (from Dec 1)|$54,054|$4,914|$901|$23.43|

* **Full prompt:** 20,000 tokens in and 1,500 out, close to her real prompt.
* **Slim prompt:** 2,000 in and 100 out, a bare "anything here?" check.
* **Only when something happens:** about 60 cheap checks a day plus 10 full decisions.

These use the list prices in `llm_provider.py`. Two things move them:

* **Our real bills run higher on two models:** DeepSeek's host costs about 1.5× list, and Grok 4.7 averaged $0.125 per call because of its reasoning tokens. Reasoning models cost more than the table shows.
* **Prompt caching would cut the per-second columns.** Second to second, most of the prompt doesn't change.

**Why calling the AI every second doesn't work:**

* **It's too slow.** A 20,000-token decision takes seconds, and longer on reasoning models; thinking models regularly miss our chat planner's 20-second limit. Calls would pile up behind each other. We don't log per-call response time, so I can't give you an exact figure.
* **Speed belongs to code.** Code reacts to a price change in milliseconds. The AI is no faster than a trained human at clicking; where it beats a human is reading more context at once.
* **Our one real-time test favored selectivity.** In the scalper sandbox, the AI version over-traded: 10 trades, 30% winners, −$34. The two mechanical strategies made one trade each, +$141 and +$66. That's a tiny sample on a buggy day, but it points to selectivity, not to watching more often.

**What could be built:** code watches every tick, and the AI decides only when a trigger fires. That's our signal-wake design (a cheap screening call, then the bots full run), except it currently checks every 5 minutes on bars. The pieces for a real-time version exist:

* the Schwab Level 2 stream for live data;
* a code watcher on that stream for triggers;
* code-placed orders with preset stops and targets, so fills happen in milliseconds;
* the AI only screening the setup and sizing it.

That keeps the AI cost in the last column whichever model you pick, so you can afford a stronger model for the decisions.

We're set up to test this with complete infrastructure for AI trading. That's what our farm project is about. We're pushing the limits beyond what others are in the realm of AI trading. If anyone wants to fund such experiments.. let me know, give us some AI cred, we'll try any idea you have

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body: honest post, and it matches what I've seen. one thought on the trigger design though: the clean test isn't AI vs other strategies, it's AI filter vs no filter on the same triggers. take every trigger the code fires, then compare taking all of them against taking only the ones the AI approves, same sizing, same exits. if the AI-approved subset doesn't beat "take everything" or a random subset of the same size, the AI is just an expensive coin flip on top of the code. and it has to be forward data, since the model has already seen the history you'd backtest on.

comments.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
comments.body:
My results so far say LLMs can do this work, on a longer horizon than day trading.

- What: LLM agents score ~1,400 US stocks nightly. Tested on the ~1,200 liquid names. Running since May 2026, clean data since Jul 10.
- Signal: 20-day rank IC of 0.18 (0.085 after sector/beta adjustment), positive on ~90% of days, May 21 to Nov 5.
- Portfolio, Jul 10 to Nov 5 (84 sessions, ~80 positions): +14.9% vs SPY −2.5% and the equal-weight universe −1.5%. Max drawdown −8.2%.
- Luck check: 0 of 200 random portfolios on the same dates came close.
- Caveats: ~4 months, one regime, about half the IC is style tilt (low beta/quality), replayed rules. A live forward test just started.

Agree it can't day-trade. Making it react faster made results worse every time I tried.

comments.author: Fluid_Expression_247
comments.body:
I think you're approaching this backward.

Why spend a year trying to get an LLM to trade by repeatedly interpreting charts when you could build a conventional trading bot and use AI to help develop, test, and refine the strategy?

You already have the infrastructure. A bot can monitor price, volume, order flow, and execute trades based on predefined conditions. You don't need an LLM making decisions every few seconds to do that.

But here's my bigger question: 
What trading edge are you actually testing?

You've spent a lot of time discussing models, token costs, latency, and execution speed. Yet I see very little about the strategy itself, its expectancy, drawdowns, or out-of-sample performance.

Your comparison of 10 AI trades against two mechanical trades proves practically nothing.

Before spending another dollar improving the infrastructure, I'd want to establish whether there's a profitable strategy to automate in the first place.

Otherwise, you're just building a more sophisticated way to lose money.

And concluding that "AI can't trade" from these experiments is a pretty big leap. What you've established is that your particular implementation hasn't demonstrated profitability. That's not the same thing.

replies.author: risk_with_rob
replies.body: Agreed. If you know how to make money, it can amplify that, and if you don’t know how to make money, it’ll amplify that as well.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The cost table is useful, and the point that code should watch every tick while the AI only gets called on a trigger makes a lot of sense. The scalper test is a fair warning too, though ten trades is too small to say much either way. A fair test of the AI-versus-mechanical question needs a few hundred trades per version, the same fees and slippage on each, and some data held back that nobody tuned on. If you want a quick way to run that kind of check, Cymetica's Backtest Labs includes fees and holds out the last part of the history.
